Baby & Child

12 Month Old Milestones: Your Baby at 1 Year

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

By 12 months, most babies pull to stand, cruise along furniture, wave bye-bye, play games like pat-a-cake, call a parent mama or dada, use a thumb and pointer finger to pick up small foods, and look for things they see you hide. All of those come from the CDC milestone checklist, which describes what 75 percent or more of children do by this age. Walking is not on the 12 month list, so a birthday without first steps is completely normal. Here is what the first year's finish line usually looks like, and what to bring to the 12 month checkup.

How to read the checklist at one year

The first birthday is a natural moment to step back and ask how your baby is growing. In 2022, the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics revised their milestone checklists so that each item reflects what 75 percent or more of children do by that age. That changes how you should read the list. If your baby does most of the 12 month items, they are keeping pace with the majority of children. If an item is missing, it is a prompt for a conversation with your pediatrician, not a verdict. Babies gain skills in bursts and in different orders, and a child who is busy mastering standing may talk a little later, then catch up quickly.

If your baby was born early, count from the due date rather than the birth date when you compare skills with a checklist. Most clinicians adjust for prematurity this way until around age two. It also helps to watch the direction of travel rather than a single snapshot. Jot down new skills with a date, or catch them on video, and look back monthly. A baby who could not pull to stand in October and cruises the couch in December is moving forward, and that trend is what clinicians care about most. And trust your own sense of your child. You watch them more closely than anyone else, and your observations are useful at every checkup.

Social and language: games, waves, and first words

Social and language milestones at this age look like play. Most 1-year-olds join simple back-and-forth games such as pat-a-cake, and they light up when you take a turn. On the communication side, most wave bye-bye, call a parent mama or dada or another special name, and understand no, which usually shows up as a brief pause or stop when you say it. The word does not need to be crisp. A baby who says mama while reaching for you, or dada when he walks in the door, is using a real word with real meaning, and that counts even when the sounds are still soft around the edges.

You do not need flashcards to support any of this. Narrate ordinary moments in short sentences, wave together at every goodbye, and answer babble as if it were conversation, because to your baby it is. Play the games your baby starts, and repeat the ones that make them laugh, since repetition is how they learn the pattern. Keep talking about what they are looking at rather than quizzing them. If you are curious about how words grow from here, and about games that build language over the second year, our guides on language development cover that stage in depth. At 12 months, showing up and taking turns is the whole job.

Hands, standing, and getting around

Two quiet cognitive milestones are easy to miss. Most 12-month-olds will put something in a container, like a block in a cup, and will look for things they see you hide, such as a toy under a blanket. Both show that your baby now understands objects exist even when they are out of sight. On the movement side, most pull to stand, cruise along furniture while holding on, and drink from an open cup when you hold it steady. Watch the hands too. The pincer grasp, picking up small bits of food between thumb and pointer finger, usually arrives around now and turns every meal into fine motor practice.

Notice what is not on the 12 month list: walking. On the revised CDC checklist, taking a few steps alone sits at 15 months, and walking well without holding on to anyone or anything sits at 18 months, so a 1-year-old who cruises but has not let go is right on schedule. Our guide on when babies walk covers the full timeline if you want the detail. To support movement now, clear a safe stretch of floor, let your baby practice barefoot, and place tempting toys on low furniture so cruising has a purpose. Skip the milestone pressure at family gatherings. Babies walk when their balance is ready, and no amount of coaxing at a birthday party moves that date.

Eating and sleeping at one year

Feeding shifts noticeably around the first birthday. Most 1-year-olds are moving toward soft versions of family foods, cut into small pieces they can pick up themselves. After 12 months, the American Academy of Pediatrics supports switching from formula to plain whole cow's milk, with around two to two and a half cups a day as a common target, and breastfeeding can continue as long as you and your baby want. Keep textures safe: skip whole grapes, whole nuts, hard raw vegetables, and other round or firm foods that can block a small airway. If cups are your current project, our guide on cup and water practice walks through the switch.

Sleep needs stay high. Most 1-year-olds do best with about 11 to 14 hours of sleep across 24 hours, counting naps. Many are still on two naps, and some start drifting toward one nap somewhere between 12 and 18 months, often with a messy few weeks in between. Expect some disruption right now even in a good sleeper. New standing skills get practiced in the crib at 2 a.m., and separation feelings often peak around the first birthday, so extra protest at bedtime is common and temporary. A steady, boring routine helps more than any product: same order, same words, same dim room, most nights.

The 12 month checkup and when to call sooner

The 12 month visit is one of the fuller ones. Your pediatrician will weigh and measure your baby and plot the growth curve, ask screening questions about the milestones above, and talk through feeding, sleep, teeth, and childproofing for a newly mobile child. The visit usually includes several immunizations, and many practices also check for anemia and lead exposure around this age; our vaccination overview covers the schedule itself. Come with questions written down, because they evaporate the moment the appointment starts. Noting new skills, sleep changes, and questions in BeMama or on paper during the weeks before makes the screening questions much easier to answer.

A few things are worth raising promptly rather than waiting for the next visit. Tell your pediatrician if your 12-month-old does not stand while holding on to something, does not search for things they see you hide, does not say single words like mama or dada, does not use gestures such as waving, or has lost skills they once had. None of these proves a problem on its own, but each one deserves a closer look, and early support works best when it starts early. If something feels off to you and no checklist captures it, say that too. Asking for a developmental screen is never an overreaction.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC milestones describe skills that most children can do by a particular age across social, language, thinking, and movement domains. They support observation and conversation but do not replace standardized developmental screening.

Individual skills vary, but caregiver concern matters. Missing several expected skills, losing a skill, or a difference in movement, communication, hearing, or vision should be discussed promptly.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to preserve dated observations, growth, activities, and questions for well-child visits. It cannot label development as normal or delayed.

When to seek help

Contact your child’s healthcare professional whenever you are concerned or notice loss of a skill. Seek urgent care for an acute change, breathing difficulty, loss of responsiveness, or seizure-like activity.

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Most 1-year-olds pull to stand, cruise, wave bye-bye, play pat-a-cake, and say mama or dada.
  • The CDC checklist shows what 75 percent or more of children do, so treat it as a guide, not a race.
  • First steps alone sit at 15 months on the revised checklist, so not walking at the birthday is on schedule.
  • After 12 months, most babies move toward family foods and whole milk and need 11 to 14 hours of sleep.
  • Call your pediatrician about no standing with support, no gestures, no single words, or any lost skills.

Frequently asked questions

What should a 12 month old be doing?

Most 12-month-olds pull to stand, cruise along furniture, wave bye-bye, play games like pat-a-cake, say mama or dada, understand no, pick up small bits with thumb and pointer finger, and look for objects they see you hide. These items come from the CDC checklist of what 75 percent or more of children do by this age. A baby missing one item is not automatically behind, but it is worth mentioning at the 12 month checkup.

When do babies say mama?

Most babies say mama or dada with real meaning by around 12 months, and many babble the sounds earlier without attaching them to a person. The word counts when it is aimed at you, such as saying mama while reaching for you. If your baby says no single words at 12 months, mention it to your pediatrician.

Is it normal for a 12 month old to not be walking?

Yes, not walking at 12 months is normal. The revised CDC checklist places taking a few steps alone at 15 months and walking without holding on at 18 months, so a 1-year-old who pulls to stand and cruises along furniture is on schedule. Do mention it to your pediatrician if your baby is not yet standing with support, or if anything about their strength or movement worries you.

What happens at the 12 month checkup?

The 12 month checkup usually includes weight, length, and head measurements, developmental screening questions, guidance on feeding and sleep, and several routine immunizations. Many practices also screen for anemia and lead exposure around this age. It is a good moment to raise anything about milestones, milk, naps, or safety, so bring your questions written down.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
